title: $2.1B AI CEO: The Beginner's Playbook to a Profitable AI Startup in 2026 | Grant Lee, CEO Gamma
aboutGuest: Grant Lee is the co-founder and CEO of Gamma, an AI presentation tool that has reached 100 million users and achieved a $2.1 billion valuation. He launched Gamma at the end of 2020 during the pandemic with two co-founders, growing the company to a team of 50 people. Prior to founding Gamma, Grant worked at Optimiz, where he met his co-founders before the company was acquired.
summary: Grant Lee built Gamma, an AI tool that turns prompts into finished presentations, into a $2.1 billion company in just 4 years starting in late 2020 during the pandemic. He shares his journey of launching with no salary, a newborn daughter, and an investor who called it "the worst idea he'd ever heard." Despite these obstacles, Gamma grew to 100 million users with a lean team of 50 people. Grant breaks down the specific strategies that got Gamma to product-market fit, including how to run a fundraise in two weeks, how to identify if an idea is worth dedicating a year of your life to, and the two signals that indicate product-market fit before revenue proves it. He emphasizes that the biggest mistake AI founders make when fundraising is not thinking about distribution and organic virality from day one, and that friends will lie about your product—the real validation comes when people put their credit card down to pay.
keyTakeaways: Choose complementary co-founders with different skill sets over trying to build alone—Grant intentionally selected founders from his previous company who brought different capabilities to balance product, engineering, and business needs
Product-market fit shows up before revenue through two signals: customers willing to pay (credit card test) and organic virality built into the product mechanics from day one, not added later

Distribution must be architected into the product foundation for AI startups facing incumbent competition—build product-led growth and organic virality into the core philosophy rather than treating it as a later-stage problem

There is no perfect timing to start a company; founders should commit when they have an idea they think about night and day, full team alignment, and family support rather than waiting for ideal circumstances

Early negative feedback from investors can be a catalyst—Grant used the harsh criticism about facing massive incumbents as motivation to build distribution-first, turning a painful message into a core product strategy

transcript.text: And you're active on X and LinkedIn, right? Try to be active on x and LinkedIn.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: And I think this is where many customers will reach out, many partnership opportunities come to fruition because of the audiences that I've built there. And again, barely scratching the surface, but more I wanna do. And I just think it feels very rewarding to start building an audience.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Yeah, just wanted to highlight it for everyone. Like 10 years ago when I was talking to entrepreneurs, the sentiment was you're not taken too seriously if you're actively posting on social media. Now, I think it's such an inevitable part of being a founder because this is how you hire, this is you learn the marketing channel, and this is just how you meet the peers.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: Totally. And I think there is a negative stigma because, you know, sometimes, you know, this is more like five, 10 years ago, where people, it almost felt like they were tooting their own horn. They want to like, oh, hey, look at me, look at me. I think you need to reframe it. Like if you have an audience and hopefully your audience overlaps with your core user base, you're trying to provide as much value to them as possible. Like you're not talking about your product all the time. In fact, you should be talking about your product very little. You should be talking about things that your audience cares about, has questions about. Obviously in this day and age, everyone's curious about how to apply AI to their work lives. How do they sift through all the noise?

How do the maintain a sense of productivity without just becoming insane because there's just too much to try to do on any one given day? So I think as a founder, you have a chance to figure out what are the, with your experience and your background and what you're building, what can you instill on your audience to inform them and keep them educated? That value in itself should be where like all the. You know, the ability to build an audience comes from, it's not about tooting your own horn, like really just talking about your product all day.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Have you looked at users who are coming from LLMs when ChatGPT recommends Gamp? Because we're tracking on a newsletter. We're just seeing crazy open rates when people find us through LLM.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: Yeah, that's actually been one that's also trending very positively, both in terms of people landing on Gamma's website, but also converting long term. So I think we're early days. It's still a relatively smaller portion of overall traffic, but it's definitely growing. And it's exciting to think about what this could look like, obviously, in a couple of years. And every business wants, obviously to diversify how customers hear about this, so that obviously you want to be able to activate multiple different channels at once. And it does feel like LLMs, you know, chats. Chat to BT, Claude, are going to be meaningful channels for us in the future.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Talk to me about pricing in general. So you start with free, then it's $8 and it goes up to $90, right? How do you come up with pricing for an AI product? And also it's dependent on how the models price themselves, right.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: Totally. So yeah, there's a lot of different moving parts. I think every startup today needs to be thinking about pricing as something that they're probably constantly experimenting with. It used to be, you know, five, 10 years ago, you kind of set it and forget it. You come up with pricing once and maybe revisit it every several years. I don't think companies today have the luxury of doing that. You constantly need to be think about, okay, the tension between like seat base versus usage base. How your product evolves, the different segments of users. So we have users that are individuals versus B2B customers that may want to buy in a completely different way. So, I mean, the honest answer for us is this is something we're still constantly experimenting with. You also want to do so in a way where pricing, you know, pricing, you're trying to align the value you provide to your user.

And then the other side of the equation is you need to be able to build a durable business. So like, are you... Actually building a business that's able to operate profitably or efficiently, the worst thing you could be doing is to be essentially selling dollars at a discount, right? If you're selling dollars a discount feels good, you're making money, but you're doing it so very unprofitably. So these are all things where constantly moving target, I think the best you can do is being willing to adapt and then user-based to kind of figure out what's the right way to balance both the value they're seeing and the cost you incur as business.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Do you have any strategies on converting customers from free into paying? Because you had this competitor, Satoma, that shut down. 5 million ARR. You had 40 million users at 20 million ARRR. So you're doing something there converting customers. Can you give advice to AI founders on how to do that?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I think it will sound generic, but it just comes back to what is the quality of the product, right? Every single category, if it's a meaningful category, there's going to be multiple competitors. And so your ability to kind of ignore the competition and focus on your users is all that really matters. Are you delivering something to them that competitors aren't either delivering on or unfocused on? Even within our own category, You know, there's many people that focus on kind of the design portion of creating a presentation, we want to focus on the communication, the storytelling. So how do we abstract design, the need for design completely away? And so you're gonna approach it differently depending on your sort of vision for this category. And then you're specifically, like your customers you're serving, what are their needs? Many different types of customers might have different needs for a presentation tool.
You need to figure out where in that space do you actually want to play.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: And your strategy has been product first from what I'm hearing, from what I'm experiencing. And you only have 50 people.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: Is it still the same? We're a little bit bigger than that, but like when we were crossing a hundred million and there are, we're 50 people. Yeah. So it was relatively small too.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Grant just said he crossed 100 million in revenue with only 50 people. This is exactly the kind of thing I love to explore in my future proof newsletter with a community of 18,000 builders and creators. Twice a week, I share the best practices from my conversations with CEOs and founders, the AI tools I'm actually using, and the skills worth learning right now. It's free. The link is in the description. The question that's very, I think, is on point for 2026. Do you think you can triple your revenue with the same amount of people? Is the technology there? Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I think the answer is yes and then the nuance is how do you triple it, right? Because we're trying to build a global business and so this means, you know, we have a lot of users in Europe, a lot of users and Asia. We still feel like we need to build the physical presence there. And so ignoring that for too long, just assuming, hey, we'll just grow from San Francisco and not grow headcount, I think would be the wrong long-term decision. And so we are trying to grow now our footprint in these different offices, which MEANS growing the team much bigger than it was obviously a year ago. So I think every business should think about what is their ambition as a business if it is to be a company that has global presence, if it to serve many different segments of users.

So like we have the prosumer end and the B2B set of users that are much different in profile, and then also serving developers through our platform or API MCP part of our business. Those all require different teams and like different places of like emphasis in terms of. Building out the complete product and platform, those require headcount. And so if we were just focused purely on prosumer, growing that as fast as possible, I think we could stay pretty lean. But if our ambition is to build a global business that can operate across segments, I think, we're gonna need a much bigger team.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: And also the question is, is there longevity in just growing the consumer business, like trying to do everything by yourself?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: Trying to do everything. Yeah, that is another tension. I think every startup is feeling today, especially today, because when it feels like you can build anything, whether you're vibe coding or just agentic coding, all the capabilities feel like they're there. When it feels like you build anything the question is, should you? And if not build everything, where are you going to focus? And so this is both the challenge and I think the opportunity building today like you have the feeling of being limitless in terms of going out there, but you also need to provide your team the right level of focus and to be kind of committed to some path of this is what we really care about and these are the things we don't and being committed to that for as long of a time horizon as possible.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Your principal is hire painfully slow. Is there a role that you wanted to have in your company, but you're not hiring because you think it's, you know, you're still like debating whether you need it or not.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I think it goes back to like every stage of company, you need to ask yourself sort of where you're at and what are the limiting factors for you to continue to grow. Oftentimes the moment a startup raises a little bit of money, they think like, okay, I need to immediately open the floodgates on sales and marketing and just hiring as many people there to build top of the funnel, build demand. But going back to is that the best way to grow an early product? Probably not. You know, it actually means. Going back to focusing on the core, like making sure the core product is so good, going back organic virality is like so good people tell all their friends about. We wanted to focus there. So rather than like open the aperture in terms of hiring across the board, when we were super early, it was all about reinvesting in the core.

Hiring the right obviously engineers, product designers. We actually probably over invested relative to what people would say like in product design. We had... It was almost a third of the company was product designers early on. And most people were like, why would you invest so much into product design? We're like, well, that matters a ton to us. So even though we were small in the relative overall head count, we were probably over indexed on product designers because we felt like that was super important. And to get true organic virality, we needed to be exceptional in that one area of that one function. And so every stage you're gonna have to look at, now that we're much bigger.

We can't afford not to hire sales and marketing because we have a massive audience to go after and we have B2B business that still requires a ton more relationship building, a much more consultative approach to actually expanding within these larger companies. And so we can just, hiring pay if only slow at this stage doesn't mean we never hire sales or marketing. It means now that we're at the stage, we feel like we've earned the right and we can gradually open up the aperture a bit more. If we had done that two or three years ago, think that would have been premature.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: How many of your employees are generalists versus specialists?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I feel like nearly all employees are what I would still define as generalists today, even though they spike in different areas. So, for instance, our head of design, exceptionally talented designer, very visual, but he also knows how to code. And he was coding even before like, vibe coding was more accessible to most designers. But the fact that he can now ship something like end-to-end, test it, like get early versions into the hands of users, that's a superpower, right? And so he can cross domains where You know, traditionally it'd be a designer or a UX researcher that does a little bit, some of this like early, you know, sort of investigation or like early research. He can do that himself, develop the early prototype, ship the early product type, get something into the hands of users to actually give feedback on, and oftentimes then ship something into production, like almost like completely end to end.

That just wasn't really possible before, but for us, like we try to look for that, the spirit of like a generalist across every function, whether it's, you now, sales, marketing, engineering, product design. And I think that allows you to have a relatively lean team that can, again, like play across multiple domains at any given point in time. And I thinking general, that just means a team that can be pretty collaborative too, because you have deeper empathy for what each function can bring to the table. And like when you're bringing something to an engineer, for instance, you've already done so much work to think through like, okay, how do I make this right? So the handoff is as seamless as possible. These things I think are hard to quantify, but when you have a team of generalists, There is some magic in working together.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: But does this model ever break or start breaking with scale? Do you feel like there will be a point in time when you will need to start hiring more specialists?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I definitely think so. But there's also the sort of competing sort of race of like, as you get bigger, you want more specialization. LLMs and AI is also getting better at being specialized in certain domains. And so there's almost like this race now of like at what point does AI also kind of fill in the remaining gap and the generals can go deep when they need to. TBD, I think certain functions like I think we're noticing, You know like within like finance and legal still pretty hard. Like you still want specialization and specific types of questions that come up. Like you don't want to just trust like an LLM, obviously to give you the right answer.

But for a lot of like sales and marketing where, your goal isn't to replace the human, it's to augment or like to really automate as much so that the human can focus on what they're good at, which is the relationship building, again, the consultative approach. You're trying to carve out, if they only have a certain number of hours in a day. You don't want them to be wasting any time like fiddling with business systems or any of that. They should be spending time with customers. And so our goal is like those generalists can help automate as much of the work that is not customer facing as possible. And the rest of the time, their specialty is to work with customers, we're trying to carve out as much time as possible for them to do that.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Yeah, that makes total sense. With all the companies deploying agents, what was the last process that you completely delegated to an agent?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I think one thing we've learned is that even with agents, you're not completely delegating things away. Like a human still needs to supervise. Still needs shade, yeah. And agents can still be fragile. They can go off course. And so I think the best cases are still where the human and agent are working hand in hand. And of course, maybe over time, you have multiple agents all working with the same human. And they can then be subdivided into different tasks. But we're still so early. We're not at the stage yet where I think any of our teammates feels like, okay, 100% agent work, now I can go do something else.

It's more like, okay, agent can actually help me provide a ton more leverage, can obviously reduce the time to complete a task, and then can help me do the things that I just would never have gotten to because my time in the day is too precious. And so there's certain aspects of that. Fast forward several years from now, then I think we're talking about maybe agents doing way more. Being much more self-directed and truly being like a partner where you can leverage the agent sort of workforce in a way that today still seems like we're still a little bit out of reach.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: What's your favorite agent?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I mean, we build a lot of things internally to help with things like customer research or even just understanding what should we be building next? Like what are pockets of things that are gonna be useful? So like taking all the input we get, we look at obviously things like churn analysis, like what are people saying? We look at when new users sign up, what are they using? How are they leveraging the product? These are all inputs. And so we wanna be able to take those inputs to say okay. Now stress test, like some of the other things we're thinking about building, like how useful is this to an end user? Where might we kind of add value in ways that we aren't even considering today? Like really being a sparring partner there.

I think those are things where you can now with much more, like every company now has so much more data they can actually work with. Taking advantage of that is really, I think where the magic really happens.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So your analyst is basically a data analyst meets product and they make decisions together. Somebody who watched this video has a startup idea, built a deck with Gamma. Can you give me their first 30 days plan, step by step?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: First 30 days plan is spend all 30 days talking to your customers. Really, I think it feels like if you're assembling the team, you need to be laser focused, customer obsessed from the very beginning, and nothing else really matters in the long run.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: It's not you wouldn't start with a co-founder

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: Well, I mean, I'm assuming if you've raised money, you have to come find us.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Had an idea and you're like, okay, I'm going to start. Is it the co-founder or you start talking to clients first to figure out who you need as a co- founder?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I personally think you shouldn't jump into the idea before the team, because the team should help inform what the idea actually is. You might have like, hey, I'm again, going back to our specific thing, which is we think like, you know, visual communication can be improved, but we weren't gonna be prescriptive into how we actually solve that. Let's, as a team, start tinkering. Like, what can our team deliver in the space that feels differentiated? And once we had that, that's when we said, okay, we feel like. There is something here, we don't know exactly what the product might look like in three or four years, but there's something here. Let's go raise money. So we have a chance to actually build this for, you know, over the next several quarters.

Once you have that, then it's about, you have the early team, you flip all of your energy into spending time with customers and early users and like testing, like, does the my thing even deliver on, you know anything that's valuable to you. And if not, let's course correct. Let's make sure we're not heading down a path of like delivering something that has zero value to you as a customer. Let's makes sure we are listening to your problems, fine tuning our own sort of understanding of the problem space, and then building the right thing over the long haul.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So for someone who came up with the idea, found the team, which is kind of hard if you are not in the ecosystem, like finding writing, but would you say this deck will help that company raise money?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: I would say yes, but it will help you sort of have the right conversations, but ultimately the investor is going to judge you based on your level of conviction and their level of conviction in your team to go after this market. So use this as a tool and every great tool can help you open the right doors and obviously to have some of the right conversations.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Can we wrap up with one final question? So if you could send one message to the founder version of yourself in 2023, when your growth was stagnating, 6K users just start there, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: It'd be some version of just hang on, you know, like every founder will go through many ups and downs. If you're surrounded by a team that, again, shares like the same level of ambition and the values and principles, then you gotta just lean on them as much as you can, and then still have belief that you can make it through. The earliest days are the hardest because it very much is, they describe it as like the idea maze. You're like bumping into wall after wall and. Not knowing if you've made any sort of meaningful traction. And so for us, it was like, hang on for as long as possible, make sure we don't lose belief in the longer-term mission of trying to help people communicate their ideas. So we feel like that should be something we could commit to for a very, very long time.
And so hanging onto that belief that we can make a difference, that's what for us actually did change the overall trajectory of the business.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: And it comes from the energy, I guess, that the product has given you, right? That was the source of that belief.

transcript.speaker: Grant Lee
transcript.text: It comes from the energy in knowing that what you're working on should help improve people's lives and the energy you're putting into it will hopefully result in amazing outcomes for your customers and users. That energy, obviously, it needs to be built up. It's like the conviction that you're constantly trying to fill up as much as possible. And if you're building the right things, I think you'll wake up every morning being excited about the things you're working on.
